extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and students interested in classical geometry and analytical-geometry problem solving (readers of a 19th‑century math journal)
extracted.subtask_description: Solve and present rigorous solutions to classical plane- and solid-geometry problems (constructive geometry, conics, analytic geometry, moment of inertia, etc.), often giving multiple methods, corollaries, and explicit equations or constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical correctness and rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions must logically derive the asserted conclusions from stated premises (e.g., 'the proposition is established', derivations of equations, elimination of variables to obtain the required relation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show step-by-step derivation: apply similar triangles, sum and reduce equations, substitute known relations, and explicitly indicate eliminations (examples: 'Eliminating n, n^ by means of (1), (4), (5) we obtain...', 'Summing these three equations, and reducing by the properties ... we get ... the proposition is established').

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy / omit trivial steps when obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: If a step or a demonstration is judged straightforward, it may be omitted with a brief remark rather than written out in full.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author/commenter may state that 'The demonstration is too obvious to require insertion.' Use this only when the omitted steps are standard consequences of earlier results or widely known propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance and simplicity of method
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions that are concise, use insightful geometric/algebraic observations, or reduce the problem with neat transformations are praised (phrases used: 'elegant theorem', 'very elegant').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer arguments that reveal structure (symmetry, harmonic relations, canonical substitutions) and that avoid unnecessary complication; elegant solutions are often singled out and sometimes printed in preference to longer computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide multiple independent methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting more than one method (First, Second, Third Solution) for the same problem is valued and frequently published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include distinct approaches — synthetic geometric, analytic/coordinate, algebraic elimination — so the reader sees different perspectives (many exercises list [First Solution], [Second Solution], [Third Solution] and note other submissions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and citation of established propositions and literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions should invoke known theorems, standard propositions, or prior literature where appropriate (e.g., 'by similar triangles', references to Horce GeometricaBy, Leslie's Geometry, Pascal's enunciations and earlier demonstrations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly name used results and give citations or references when relying on previously published facts or commonly known theorems; this situates the solution within established knowledge and saves space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle degenerate and configuration cases explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: State and treat exceptional configurations and necessary constructions (for instance 'produced if necessary', or distinguishing when diagonals meet in one point versus two-and-two intersections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify whether lines are to be produced, whether intersections are assumed finite, and consider alternate cases (case divisions as in Pascal's Theorem: when AD, BE, CF meet in one point vs. meet two-and-two).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose convenient coordinates/axes and give explicit equations
rubrics_metrics.description: When using analytic methods, select axes and origins to simplify computations (examples: 'Take the diameter of the semicircle for the axis of x, and one of its extremities for the origin') and produce explicit equation(s) of the locus or surface (circles, spheroids, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State coordinates of key points, write down the resulting equations, perform eliminations and simplifications to arrive at canonical forms (e.g., 'x^2 + y^2 - 2r(x - t/)= 0' or 'equation to a prolate spheroid').

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive corollaries and state consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: After proving main relations, extract corollaries and related formulae (e.g., area relations, perpendicular-sum identities), and note intimate relations to other known results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how the main result implies secondary formulae: label them 'Cor.' or present alternate equivalent forms ('Cor. From (I) we have the relation ... Or ... where A denotes the area of the triangle').

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity in algebraic manipulation (elimination/substitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carry out algebraic eliminations and substitutions transparently (examples: elimination of variables by combining numbered equations; comparing coefficients after expansion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number intermediate equations, indicate which are combined or subtracted, and state the elimination steps explicitly: 'multiplying out and comparing coefficients', 'eliminating p from these equations, we obtain ...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include diagrams or indicate geometric configuration when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometric solutions rely on diagrams or on explicit descriptions of configuration (poles/polars, intersections, midpoints, axes) to make the argument intelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either supply a diagram or give clear coordinate/point descriptions (e.g., 'Join the opposite angles ... by drawing the diagonals AD, BE, CF intersecting in L, M, N; and parallel ... draw the sero‑diameters OP, OR, OQ'). When the visual is essential, note its role in the proportionality or transversal arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualization and historical comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: When proposing or proving classical theorems (e.g., Pascal's Theorem), situate the demonstration among previous geometric and analytical proofs and remark on differences in enunciation or method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List prior demonstrations, note whether the new proof establishes precisely Pascal's original statement or a modern reformulation, and give references ('All the geometrical demonstrations of Pascal's Theorem which have come to my knowledge are cited below').

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce explicit constructive steps where applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: For constructive geometry problems, show how to build the required points/lines (e.g., bisect chords, draw perpendiculars, bisect segments to find centers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the straight-edge/compass steps or coordinate construction that yields the object: 'Let ABCD be the given circle, in which draw any chord AC; bisect it in P ... Draw DBP at right angles to AC ... bisect DB in O ... and O will be the centre of the circle.'
